q: In Julia, let a = [[3 6 8]; [7 9 2]; [-1 0 4]] (a $3\times 3$ matrix). What does a[[1, end], 2] return?
options: The vector [7, 9, 2]: the whole second row
The vector [2, 4]: a 0-based reading (rows 2 and 3 of the third column)
The vector [6, 0]: the entries of column 2 in the first and last rows
explain: Julia indexing is 1-based; the first index selects rows and the second columns. [1, end] picks rows 1 and 3, and column 2 of the matrix is $(6, 9, 0)$, so the result is the vector $[6, 0]$ (the book's answer; a[[1, 3], 2] is equivalent).

q: Solve $\min\ x+y$ subject to $x\ge 8.2\,y$, $y\ge 2$ when $x\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $y\in\mathbb{N}$ (nonnegative integers). What is the optimal objective value?
explain: With $y=2$ we need $x\ge 16.4$, i.e. $x=17$: objective $19$ (and $x+4y=25$). Any $y\ge 3$ needs $x\ge 24.6$ and costs at least $28$. The continuous version of the model is the LP relaxation: its value $18.4$ is a lower bound, and since its optimum $x=16.4$ is fractional the integer optimum is strictly larger.

q: Consider the production model with periods $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$: $$\min \sum_{t\in T}(c_t y_t+d_t x_t)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_t\le 50\,y_t\ \ \forall t,\qquad z_1=x_1-e_1,\qquad z_t=z_{t-1}+x_t-e_t\ \ (t=2,3,4),$$ with $x_t\ge 0$, $z_t\ge 0$, $y_t\in\{0,1\}$ and data $c=(15.2,\ 14.8,\ 15.9,\ 14.3)$, $d=(0.2,\ 0.2,\ 0.1,\ 0.6)$, $e=(5,\ 40,\ 20,\ 50)$. What is the optimal objective value?
explain: $x_t$ is the production (at most 50, only if $y_t=1$), $z_t$ the stock and $e_t$ the demand. Cumulative demands are $5, 45, 65, 115$, so period 1 must produce and at least three set-ups are needed ($2\cdot 50\lt 115$). Pattern $y=(1,1,1,0)$: fixed cost $45.9$; produce 50 in period 3 (unit cost 0.1) and 65 in periods 1-2 (unit cost 0.2): $5+13=18$, total $63.9$. The other feasible patterns cost more: $(1,0,1,1)$: $69.4$; $(1,1,0,1)$: $73.3$; $(1,1,1,1)$: $78.2$. (Recomputed by enumerating $y$ and solving the LP in $x,z$.)

q: Nurse scheduling. A day has 12 two-hour periods $1,\dots,12$ (period 1 = 0h-2h) and the same schedule repeats every day. A nurse starting in period $t$ works periods $t$ and $t+1$, has a break in period $t+2$, then works periods $t+3$ and $t+4$ (indices cyclic modulo 12). Let $x_t$ be the number of nurses starting in period $t$ and $r_t$ the number of nurses required in period $t$. Which constraint guarantees the coverage of period 5 (8h-10h)?
explain: A nurse who starts in period $s$ is on duty in period 5 exactly when $5\in\{s,\ s+1,\ s+3,\ s+4\}$, i.e. $s\in\{5,4,2,1\}$. The nurse starting in period 3 is on break in period 5, so $x_3$ must not appear; the option with $x_6,x_8,x_9$ looks forward instead of backward. The full model is $\min\sum_t x_t$ s.t. $x_t+x_{t-1}+x_{t-3}+x_{t-4}\ge r_t$ for all $t$ (indices modulo 12), $x_t\in\mathbb{Z}_+$. The formulation is not printed in the book; for its requirement table $r=(15,14,14,17,22,20,10,20,18,15,20,20)$ this cyclic model needs 57 nurses (solver check), consistent with the book's remark that 55 are not enough.

q: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be binary variables. Which set of linear constraints enforces $c=a\lor b$ (logical OR)?
explain: $c\ge a$ and $c\ge b$ force $c=1$ as soon as one of them is 1; $c\le a+b$ forces $c=0$ when both are 0. The set $c\le a$, $c\le b$, $c\ge a+b-1$ is the linearisation of AND; $c\ge a+b$ is infeasible for $a=b=1$; $c\le a+b$ alone never forces $c=1$. (Standard answer; the book states the exercise without solution.)

q: For binary $a_1,\dots,a_n$ and $c$, the compact formulation $n\,c\ge\sum_{i}a_i,\ \ c\le\sum_i a_i$ of $c=a_1\lor\dots\lor a_n$ has the same LP relaxation as the disaggregated formulation $c\ge a_i\ (i=1,\dots,n),\ \ c\le\sum_i a_i$.
explain: Both are correct for binary values, but the compact one is weaker. Summing $c\ge a_i$ over $i$ gives $n\,c\ge\sum_i a_i$, so the disaggregated relaxation is contained in the compact one; the inclusion is strict: with $n=3$, $a=(1,0,0)$, $c=\tfrac13$ satisfies $3c\ge 1$ and $c\le 1$ but violates $c\ge a_1$. Fewer constraints, weaker relaxation.

q: For binary variables $a$ and $b$, which linear constraint states that the implication $a\Rightarrow b$ holds?
explain: The only combination to exclude is $(a,b)=(1,0)$, and $a\le b$ excludes exactly that one. $a\ge b$ encodes $b\Rightarrow a$, $a+b\le 1$ says 'not both', and $a+b\ge 1$ is the OR. (Standard answer; no solution printed in the book.)

q: Let $x\in[0,100]$ be continuous and $y$ binary. Which single linear constraint models 'if $y=1$ then $x=100$' while leaving $x$ free in $[0,100]$ when $y=0$?
explain: Together with the bound $x\le 100$, $x\ge 100y$ gives $x=100$ when $y=1$ and is void when $y=0$. $x\le 100y$ models 'if $y=0$ then $x=0$'; $x=100y$ also forces $x=0$ when $y=0$ (too strong); $x\ge 100(1-y)$ triggers on $y=0$ instead of $y=1$.

q: A variable $x\ge 0$ must take a value in $\{0\}\cup[m,M]$ with $0\lt m\lt M$ (semicontinuous variable). With a binary variable $y$, which constraints model this?
explain: $y=0$ gives $x=0$ and $y=1$ gives $m\le x\le M$. With $x\le My$ only, values in $(0,m)$ remain possible; $m\le x\le My$ makes $x=0$ impossible; $m(1-y)\le x\le My$ is infeasible for $y=0$ and allows $[0,M]$ for $y=1$.

q: Let $y\in[0,100]$ be continuous and $x$ binary. Give linear constraints enforcing $x=1$ if $y\ge 50$ and $x=0$ otherwise, and explain how the model behaves at $y=50$.
model: With a small tolerance $\varepsilon\gt 0$: $$y\ge 50\,x,\qquad y\le 50+50\,x-\varepsilon\,(1-x).$$ If $x=1$: $50\le y\le 100$. If $x=0$: $0\le y\le 50-\varepsilon$. Hence $y\ge 50$ forces $x=1$ and $y\le 50-\varepsilon$ forces $x=0$ (values strictly between $50-\varepsilon$ and $50$ are excluded). Without the tolerance, i.e. with $y\le 50+50x$, both $x=0$ and $x=1$ are feasible at exactly $y=50$: a linear model with closed constraints cannot express the strict inequality $y\lt 50$, so the boundary point is ambiguous unless an $\varepsilon$ is introduced.
rubric: A constraint forcing $y\ge 50$ when $x=1$ (e.g. $y\ge 50x$)
A big-M constraint forcing $y$ below 50 when $x=0$ (e.g. $y\le 50+50x$, with $M=50$)
States that without a tolerance both values of $x$ are feasible at $y=50$
Explains that strict inequalities cannot be modelled; an $\varepsilon$ fixes the boundary at the price of excluding a small interval
explain: Check by cases $x=0$ and $x=1$: each constraint must be binding in one case and redundant (thanks to the bounds $0\le y\le 100$) in the other.

q: A piecewise-linear approximation of $f(x)=x^3+\log_2 x$ uses breakpoints every $0.5$ between $2$ and $9.5$; two consecutive breakpoints are $(4,\ 66)$ and $(4.5,\ 93.295)$. In the convex-combination model ($x=\sum_k a_k\lambda_k$, $y=\sum_k f_k\lambda_k$, $\sum_k\lambda_k=1$, $\lambda\ge 0$, only two adjacent $\lambda_k$ nonzero), which value of $y$ corresponds to $x=4.2$?
explain: $4.2=0.6\cdot 4+0.4\cdot 4.5$, so the two active weights are $0.6$ and $0.4$ and $y=0.6\cdot 66+0.4\cdot 93.295=39.6+37.318=76.918$. (The true value is $f(4.2)\approx 76.16$: the chord of a convex function overestimates it.) In the MILP, binaries select the active segment so that only two adjacent weights are positive.

q: A player has 1000 coins to buy any number of warriors of five types with (strength, price): type 1: $(1,3)$; type 2: $(3,3)$; type 3: $(7,6)$; type 4: $(8,7)$; type 5: $(10,9)$. With $n_i\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ warriors of type $i$ the model is $\max\ n_1+3n_2+7n_3+8n_4+10n_5$ s.t. $3n_1+3n_2+6n_3+7n_4+9n_5\le 1000$. What is the maximum total strength?
explain: The best strength/price ratio is type 3 ($7/6$), so the LP relaxation gives $1000\cdot 7/6\approx 1166.67$ and the integer optimum is at most $1166$. This value is attained: 165 warriors of type 3 (990 coins, strength 1155), one of type 4 (7 coins, 8) and one of type 2 (3 coins, 3) use exactly 1000 coins for a strength of 1166. The rounded relaxation bound therefore proves optimality (also checked with a knapsack DP). The book asks only for the formulation.

q: Files cannot be split across drives. There are $n_2$ files of 2 GB, $n_3$ files of 3 GB, $n_5$ files of 5 GB and $n_7$ files of 7 GB. (a) Formulate as an integer program the problem of storing all files on a minimum number of 16 GB flash drives. (b) Adapt the model when 32 GB drives cost 9 euros, 16 GB drives cost 5 euros and 8 GB drives cost 3 euros and the total cost is minimised.
model: (a) Let $S=\{2,3,5,7\}$ and let $K$ be an upper bound on the number of drives (e.g. $K=n_2+n_3+n_5+n_7$). Variables: $y_k\in\{0,1\}$ (drive $k$ is used) and $x_{sk}\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ (number of files of size $s$ on drive $k$). $$\min\sum_{k=1}^{K}y_k\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{k=1}^{K}x_{sk}=n_s\ \ \forall s\in S,\qquad\sum_{s\in S}s\,x_{sk}\le 16\,y_k\ \ \forall k.$$ (b) Index potential drives by a type $\tau\in\{32,16,8\}$ with costs $c_{32}=9$, $c_{16}=5$, $c_{8}=3$; variables $y_{\tau k}\in\{0,1\}$ and $x_{s\tau k}\in\mathbb{Z}_+$: $$\min\sum_{\tau}\sum_{k}c_\tau\,y_{\tau k}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{\tau}\sum_{k}x_{s\tau k}=n_s\ \ \forall s,\qquad\sum_{s\in S}s\,x_{s\tau k}\le\tau\,y_{\tau k}\ \ \forall\tau,k.$$ This is a bin-packing model; using one binary variable per individual file instead of integer counts per size is also correct.
rubric: Binary 'drive used' variables and assignment variables (counts per size or one binary per file)
Every file stored exactly once: $\sum_k x_{sk}=n_s$
Capacity linked to the use variable: $\sum_s s\,x_{sk}\le 16\,y_k$
Objective (a): number of drives used
(b): drive types with capacities 32/16/8 in the capacity constraint and costs 9/5/3 in the objective
explain: The capacity constraint with $y_k$ on the right-hand side both limits the load and forces $y_k=1$ whenever something is stored on drive $k$ (a fixed-charge link). Not solved in the book; the model is worked.

q: Unit commitment. Over periods $t=1,\dots,T$ a company operates plants $i=1,\dots,P$ with maximum power $P_i^{\max}$ and must satisfy the demand $d_t$ in every period. Using plant $i$ in period $t$ costs a fixed amount $f_{t,i}$ plus $p_{t,i}$ per unit produced; a start-up cost $g_{t,i}$ is paid each time plant $i$ runs in period $t$ after being down in period $t-1$; and each time a plant starts it must run for at least four consecutive periods. Formulate the cost minimisation as a mixed-integer program.
model: Variables: $u_{t,i}\in\{0,1\}$ (plant $i$ on in $t$), $v_{t,i}\in\{0,1\}$ (plant $i$ starts in $t$), $q_{t,i}\ge 0$ (production). $$\min\sum_{t}\sum_{i}\big(f_{t,i}\,u_{t,i}+p_{t,i}\,q_{t,i}+g_{t,i}\,v_{t,i}\big)$$ subject to: $\sum_i q_{t,i}=d_t$ for all $t$ (demand); $q_{t,i}\le P_i^{\max}u_{t,i}$ (production only when on); $v_{t,i}\ge u_{t,i}-u_{t-1,i}$ (start-up detection, $u_{0,i}$ given by the initial state); and $u_{\tau,i}\ge v_{t,i}$ for $\tau=t,\dots,\min(t+3,T)$ (a start in $t$ keeps the plant on for four periods). Since $g\ge 0$, $v_{t,i}=1$ at an optimum only when a start really occurs.
rubric: On/off binaries with $q_{t,i}\le P_i^{\max}u_{t,i}$
Demand satisfied in every period
Start-up variable with $v_{t,i}\ge u_{t,i}-u_{t-1,i}$ and start-up cost in the objective
Minimum up time: a start in $t$ forces $u=1$ in periods $t,\dots,t+3$
Objective = fixed + variable + start-up costs
explain: The key modelling devices are the big-M link between production and the on/off binary and the logical link 'start = on now and off before'. Exam question (September 2016) given without solution in the book; the model is worked.

q: A MILP for a shortest path with node opening times uses binaries $x_{ij}$ (arc $(i,j)$ used), times $t_i\ge r_i$ with $t_1=0$, flow-conservation constraints selecting a path from node 1 to node $n$, the objective $\min t_n$, and the linking constraints $t_j\ge t_i+c_{ij}\,x_{ij}$ for all arcs $(i,j)$. What is the flaw of this linking constraint and its repair?
options: For an unused arc it still imposes $t_j\ge t_i$, so nodes off the path can delay $t_n$; use $t_j\ge t_i+c_{ij}-M(1-x_{ij})$
It is nonlinear because it multiplies $c_{ij}$ by $x_{ij}$; replace it by $t_j\ge t_i+c_{ij}$ for all arcs
It does not prevent subtours; add subtour-elimination constraints and keep it unchanged
It should be an equality $t_j=t_i+c_{ij}x_{ij}$ so that no waiting is allowed
explain: With $x_{ij}=0$ the constraint reduces to $t_j\ge t_i$: times are propagated along every arc, used or not. A node $i$ outside the chosen path with a late opening time $r_i$ then forces $t_j\ge r_i$ for its successors and can overestimate $t_n$. A big-M term switches the constraint off on unused arcs. ($c_{ij}x_{ij}$ is linear since $c_{ij}$ is a constant; waiting at a node must stay possible, so an equality would be wrong.) The formulation is the book's; the flaw was identified when working the exercise.

q: A binary knapsack with 5 items has values $(3,4,6,5,8)$, weights $(412, 507, 714, 671, 920)$ and capacity $1794$. Why is this instance awkward for the classical dynamic program indexed by the capacity?
options: Its running time is $O(nC)$ (items times capacity), which is only pseudo-polynomial: about 1800 capacity states per item for a tiny input
The DP is exponential in the number of items, and $n=5$ is already too many
The DP is only correct when all weights are smaller than the capacity divided by $n$
The DP requires the LP relaxation to have an integer optimum, which fails here
explain: The DP table has one column per capacity value, so the work is proportional to $n\cdot C=5\cdot 1794$, i.e. it grows with the magnitude of the numbers (exponential in their encoding length), not only with the number of items. The book's remedy is the 'dual' DP indexed by value (total value only 26).

q: Consider the integer program $\max\ 9x+5y$ subject to $4x+9y\le 35$, $x\le 6$, $x-3y\ge 1$, $3x+2y\le 19$, $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$. What is the optimal value of the LP relaxation solved at the root node of branch-and-bound?
explain: At $x=6$ the constraints give $y\le 11/9$, $y\le 5/3$ and $y\le 1/2$; the last one ($3x+2y\le 19$) is binding, so the LP optimum is the vertex $(6,\ 0.5)$ with value $54+2.5=56.5$. It is optimal because $(9,5)=1.5\,(1,0)+2.5\,(3,2)$ is a nonnegative combination of the normals of the two binding constraints.

q: Solve by branch-and-bound: $\max\ 9x+5y$ subject to $4x+9y\le 35$, $x\le 6$, $x-3y\ge 1$, $3x+2y\le 19$, $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$. What is the optimal objective value?
explain: Root LP: $(6,\ 0.5)$, value $56.5$; branch on $y$. Node $y\le 0$: LP optimum $(6,0)$, value $54$, integer: incumbent. Node $y\ge 1$: LP optimum $(17/3,\ 1)$, value $56$; branch on $x$: $x\le 5$ gives $(5,\ 4/3)$ with value $51.67\lt 54$ (pruned by bound) and $x\ge 6$ is infeasible ($18+2\gt 19$). The optimum is $(x,y)=(6,0)$, the book's answer, with value $54$.

q: For $\max\ 9x+5y$ subject to $4x+9y\le 35$, $x\le 6$, $x-3y\ge 1$, $3x+2y\le 19$, $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$, branch-and-bound has found the incumbent $(6,0)$ of value 54 in the node $y\le 0$. The sibling node $y\ge 1$ has LP optimum $(17/3,\ 1)$ of value 56 and is branched on $x$. What happens to its two children?
options: $x\le 5$: LP value about $51.67$, pruned by bound; $x\ge 6$: infeasible
$x\le 5$: LP value about $51.67$, must be branched further; $x\ge 6$: infeasible
Both children have integer LP solutions that improve the incumbent
explain: Child $x\le 5$, $y\ge 1$: at $x=5$, $y\le\min(5/3,\ 4/3,\ 2)=4/3$, value $45+20/3\approx 51.67\lt 54$, so it is pruned by bound without further branching. Child $x\ge 6$ (so $x=6$) with $y\ge 1$: $3\cdot 6+2\cdot 1=20\gt 19$, infeasible. The search ends with optimum 54.

q: Consider the integer program $\max\ 2x+3y$ subject to $-\tfrac23x+y\le\tfrac52$, $\tfrac13x+y\le\tfrac92$, $2x+y\le 14$, $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$. What is the optimal value of its LP relaxation?
explain: The LP optimum is at the intersection of $\tfrac13x+y=\tfrac92$ and $2x+y=14$: subtracting gives $\tfrac53x=9.5$, so $x=5.7$, $y=2.6$ and the value is $11.4+7.8=19.2$. Optimality: $(2,3)=\tfrac{12}{5}(\tfrac13,1)+\tfrac35(2,1)$ with nonnegative multipliers.

q: Branch-and-bound on $\max\ 2x+3y$ subject to $-\tfrac23x+y\le\tfrac52$, $\tfrac13x+y\le\tfrac92$, $2x+y\le 14$, $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$: the root LP optimum is $(5.7,\ 2.6)$. Branching on $x$ gives node A ($x\ge 6$) with LP optimum $(6,2)$ of value 18, and node B ($x\le 5$) with LP optimum $(5,\ 17/6)$ of value 18.5. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Node B must be branched on $y$, because its bound $18.5$ exceeds the incumbent $18$
Node A is pruned by bound and the search continues in node B only
Node B is infeasible, so $(6,2)$ is optimal
$(6,2)$ is optimal: integer points have integer objective values, so node B cannot contain anything better than $\lfloor 18.5\rfloor=18$
explain: Node A gives the integer solution $(6,2)$ of value 18 (the book's answer). Node B's bound is 18.5, but the objective $2x+3y$ is an integer for integer $x,y$, so the bound can be rounded down to 18: node B cannot improve the incumbent and is pruned by bound. (Without this rounding argument one would branch on $y$ in node B and find values at most 18.)

q: A partial branch-and-bound tree shows the LP value of each node: #0: 25; its children #1: 27 and #2: 26; children of #1: #3: 28 and #4: 30; children of #2: #5: 27 and #6: 35 (LP solution integer); children of #4: #7: 31 (LP solution integer) and #8: infeasible. Nodes #3 and #5 have not been branched yet. The problem is a minimisation. With gap $=$ (upper bound $-$ lower bound) / upper bound, what is the current optimality gap in percent?
explain: Upper bound = best integer solution $=\min(35,31)=31$. Lower bound = smallest LP value among the leaves that are still open $=\min(28,27)=27$. Gap $=(31-27)/31=12.9\%$, as printed in the book.

q: A partial branch-and-bound tree shows the LP value of each node: #0: 25; its children #1: 27 and #2: 26; children of #1: #3: 28 and #4: 30; children of #2: #5: 27 and #6: 35 (LP solution integer); children of #4: #7: 31 (LP solution integer) and #8: infeasible. Nodes #3 and #5 have not been branched yet. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a maximisation; the incumbent is #6 with value 35 and every other leaf can be pruned
It is a minimisation; #3 is pruned by bound because $28\gt 27$, so only #5 remains
It is a minimisation (LP values increase down the tree); the incumbent is #7 with value 31, and #3 and #5 must still be explored
It is a minimisation; the search is over because two integer solutions have been found
explain: Adding branching constraints can only worsen the LP value; here the values increase from parent to child, so the problem is a minimisation and LP values are lower bounds. #6 (35) and #7 (31) are integer: the incumbent is 31. #8 is pruned by infeasibility. #3 (28) and #5 (27) have bounds below 31 and may still contain better solutions, so both remain open (the book's answer).

q: In a partial branch-and-bound tree, each node shows an upper bound (top number) and, when known, a lower bound (bottom number). Root: 52.7. Its children: 52.3 and 49.9. Children of the node 52.3: a node with 50.1 and a node marked $-\infty$. Children of the node 49.9: a node with 47 on top and 47 at the bottom, and a node with 49.7. Children of the node 49.7: a node with 44 on top and 44 at the bottom, and a node with 43.7. What is the sense of optimisation and the tightest interval known for the optimal value $z^*$?
explain: The relaxation bounds are upper bounds and decrease down the tree, and $-\infty$ marks an infeasible node: it is a maximisation. Lower bound = best feasible value $=47$ (the node 44/44 is a worse solution). Upper bound = largest upper bound among the leaves $=\max(50.1,\ -\infty,\ 47,\ 44,\ 43.7)=50.1$. The values 52.7 and 49.7 belong to internal nodes whose children give tighter bounds. (No solution printed in the book.)

q: In a partial branch-and-bound tree, each node shows an upper bound (top number) and, when known, a lower bound (bottom number). Root: 52.7. Its children: 52.3 and 49.9. Children of the node 52.3: a node with 50.1 and a node marked $-\infty$. Children of the node 49.9: a node with 47 on top and 47 at the bottom, and a node with 49.7. Children of the node 49.7: a node with 44 on top and 44 at the bottom, and a node with 43.7. The problem is a maximisation. Which nodes must still be explored to find an optimal solution?
options: The leaves with upper bounds 50.1 and 43.7
Only the leaf with upper bound 50.1
Only the leaf with 43.7, because it is the deepest open node
None: the node 47/47 already proves optimality
explain: The incumbent is 47. The leaf 50.1 may contain a better solution ($50.1\gt 47$). The leaf 43.7 is pruned by bound ($43.7\lt 47$), the node $-\infty$ by infeasibility, and the nodes 47/47 and 44/44 are solved (pruned by optimality). Optimality is not proved yet because the global upper bound is still 50.1.

q: In a partial branch-and-bound tree, each node shows an upper bound (top number) and, when known, a lower bound (bottom number). Root: 52.7. Its children: 52.3 and 49.9. Children of the node 52.3: a node with 50.1 and a node marked $-\infty$. Children of the node 49.9: a node with 47 on top and 47 at the bottom, and a node with 49.7. Children of the node 49.7: a node with 44 on top and 44 at the bottom, and a node with 43.7. The problem is a maximisation. Suppose the two best solutions are wanted, not only the best one. Which nodes should be explored further, and why?
model:
Two feasible values are known, 47 and 44, so the second-best value is at least 44.
  • Leaf 50.1: must be explored (it may contain solutions better than 47, or between 44 and 47).
  • Node 47/47: its relaxation optimum is feasible, but the same subproblem may contain other feasible solutions with value between 44 and 47; it must be explored further (branching so that the solution already found is excluded).
  • Leaf 43.7: every solution there is worth at most $43.7\lt 44$, it stays pruned.
  • Node 44/44: its other solutions are worth at most 44 and cannot improve on the known pair (47, 44).
  • Node $-\infty$: infeasible.
rubric: The second-best value is currently at least 44 (known solutions 47 and 44)
Leaf 50.1 must be explored
Node 47/47 must be re-opened: other solutions of that subproblem can be second best
Leaf 43.7 stays pruned because $43.7\lt 44$; the infeasible node stays pruned
explain: For the $k$ best solutions the pruning threshold is the $k$-th best known value, and a node 'pruned by optimality' only tells us its best solution, not its second best.

q: A partial branch-and-bound tree gives, for each node, a lower bound on the optimal value of its subproblem and sometimes an upper bound. Node 0 (root): upper 31, lower 20.8. Node 1 (child of 0): lower 22.1. Node 2 (child of 0): lower 29.2. Node 3 (child of 1): upper 29, lower 29. Node 4 (child of 1): lower 22.2. Node 5 (child of 4): lower 23.7. Node 6 (child of 4): infeasible. The problem is a minimisation. What is the tightest lower bound on the optimal value of the full problem?
explain: The leaves are nodes 2, 3, 5 and 6. The global lower bound is the smallest lower bound among the feasible leaves: $\min(29.2,\ 29,\ 23.7)=23.7$. The best upper bound is 29 (the solution of node 3, better than the 31 known at the root), so $23.7\le z^*\le 29$, a gap of about $18.3\%$.

q: A partial branch-and-bound tree gives, for each node, a lower bound on the optimal value of its subproblem and sometimes an upper bound. Node 0 (root): upper 31, lower 20.8. Node 1 (child of 0): lower 22.1. Node 2 (child of 0): lower 29.2. Node 3 (child of 1): upper 29, lower 29. Node 4 (child of 1): lower 22.2. Node 5 (child of 4): lower 23.7. Node 6 (child of 4): infeasible. Which statement is correct?
options: Minimisation; nodes 2 and 5 both still have to be explored
Maximisation; only node 2 still has to be explored
Minimisation; only node 5 still has to be explored (node 2 is pruned by bound since $29.2\gt 29$)
Minimisation; nothing is left to explore because node 3 has equal bounds
explain: Lower bounds come from relaxations and increase down the tree, upper bounds from feasible solutions: it is a minimisation. The incumbent is 29 (node 3). Node 2 cannot contain a solution better than 29.2, so it is pruned by bound; node 3 is solved; node 6 is infeasible; node 5 (bound $23.7\lt 29$) is the only node left.

q: A partial branch-and-bound tree gives, for each node, a lower bound on the optimal value of its subproblem and sometimes an upper bound. Node 0 (root): upper 31, lower 20.8. Node 1 (child of 0): lower 22.1. Node 2 (child of 0): lower 29.2. Node 3 (child of 1): upper 29, lower 29. Node 4 (child of 1): lower 22.2. Node 5 (child of 4): lower 23.7. Node 6 (child of 4): infeasible. The problem is a minimisation with incumbent 29 (node 3). If the two best solutions are wanted, which leaves can potentially contain the second-best solution?
explain: Leaf 5 is unexplored (bound 23.7). Leaf 2 only contains solutions of value at least 29.2: useless for the best solution, but possibly the second best. Leaf 3 is solved for its best solution (29), yet other solutions of the same subproblem, with value at least 29, may be second best. Leaf 6 is infeasible.

q: Name the three ways in which a node can be pruned in branch-and-bound.
a:
• By bound: the node's relaxation value is not better than the incumbent.
  • By optimality: the relaxation solution is integer-feasible (it becomes the incumbent if it improves it).
  • By infeasibility: the node's relaxation is infeasible.

q: Two simple node-selection strategies in branch-and-bound are depth-first and breadth-first search. Which statement describes their effect on the bounds?
options: Depth-first mainly improves the primal bound (it reaches integer solutions quickly); breadth-first mainly improves the dual bound
Depth-first mainly improves the dual bound; breadth-first mainly improves the primal bound
Both improve only the dual bound; primal bounds come exclusively from heuristics
Breadth-first is the strategy that reaches a first integer solution in the fewest nodes
explain: Diving deep adds many branching constraints quickly, so leaves with integer solutions (incumbents, i.e. primal bounds) are reached early. Breadth-first treats all shallow nodes first, which raises the worst remaining relaxation value (the dual bound) but usually finds feasible solutions late. This is the book's answer.

q: Two formulations with LP relaxations $P_1$ and $P_2$ describe the same set of integer points, and you have shown $P_1\subseteq P_2$. What is enough to conclude that $P_1$ is strictly stronger?
options: Exhibit one integer point that belongs to $P_2$ but not to $P_1$
Check that one particular point of $P_1$ also belongs to $P_2$
Exhibit one point of $P_2$ (necessarily fractional) that violates a constraint of $P_1$
Show that $P_1$ has more constraints than $P_2$
explain: $P_1\subsetneq P_2$ needs a point in $P_2\setminus P_1$. Because both formulations have the same integer points, such a point must be fractional. Checking a single point of $P_1$ proves nothing, and the number of constraints says nothing about inclusion.

q: Uncapacitated facility location with clients $C$, facilities $F$, variables $x_j$ (facility $j$ open) and $y_{ij}$ (client $i$ served by $j$), and assignment constraints $\sum_{j\in F}y_{ij}=1$ for all $i\in C$. Formulation A links the variables with $y_{ij}\le x_j$ for all $i\in C$, $j\in F$; formulation B uses the aggregated constraints $\sum_{i\in C}y_{ij}\le |C|\,x_j$ for all $j\in F$. How do the LP relaxations compare?
options: B is strictly stronger than A
A is strictly stronger than B
explain: Summing $y_{ij}\le x_j$ over $i$ gives B's constraint, so $P_A\subseteq P_B$. The inclusion is strict: with two clients and two facilities, $y_{11}=y_{22}=1$, $x_1=x_2=\tfrac12$ satisfies B ($1\le 2\cdot\tfrac12$) but not A ($1\gt\tfrac12$). The price is $|C|\,|F|$ linking constraints instead of $|F|$. This is the book's conclusion.

q: Uncapacitated facility location with clients $C$, facilities $F$, variables $x_j$ (facility $j$ open) and $y_{ij}$ (client $i$ served by $j$), and assignment constraints $\sum_{j\in F}y_{ij}=1$ for all $i\in C$. Formulation A links the variables with $y_{ij}\le x_j$ for all $i\in C$, $j\in F$; formulation B uses the aggregated constraints $\sum_{i\in C}y_{ij}\le |C|\,x_j$ for all $j\in F$. Both relaxations also contain $0\le x_j\le 1$ and $y_{ij}\ge 0$. Prove that formulation A is strictly stronger than formulation B.
model: Inclusion. Let $(x,y)\in P_A$. Summing $y_{ij}\le x_j$ over $i\in C$ gives $\sum_{i\in C}y_{ij}\le |C|\,x_j$; all other constraints are common, so $(x,y)\in P_B$ and $P_A\subseteq P_B$. Strictness. Take $C=\{1,2\}$, $F=\{1,2\}$, $y_{11}=y_{22}=1$, $y_{12}=y_{21}=0$, $x_1=x_2=\tfrac12$. The assignment constraints hold and $\sum_i y_{i1}=1\le 2\cdot\tfrac12$ (same for $j=2$), so the point is in $P_B$; but $y_{11}=1\gt\tfrac12=x_1$, so it is not in $P_A$. Hence $P_A\subsetneq P_B$. (For binary $x$ both linkings describe the same integer solutions, so both formulations are valid.)
rubric: Shows $P_A\subseteq P_B$ by summing the disaggregated constraints over the clients
Gives a fractional point satisfying the aggregated constraints
Checks that this point violates some $y_{ij}\le x_j$
Concludes strict inclusion (same integer points, smaller relaxation)
explain: The book states the conclusion only; the proof follows its recipe: constraints of the stronger formulation imply those of the weaker, plus one fractional separating point.

q: Exam timetabling: $x_{it}=1$ if exam $i\in L$ takes place on day $t\in T$; $C(k)$ is the set of courses of student $k\in S$; every exam is scheduled once, $\sum_{t\in T}x_{it}=1$. To forbid two exams of the same student on the same day, formulation 1 uses $\sum_{i\in C(k)}x_{it}\le 1$ for all $k\in S$, $t\in T$, and formulation 2 uses $x_{it}+x_{jt}\le 1$ for all $k\in S$, $t\in T$ and all pairs $i\ne j$ in $C(k)$. Which formulation is better? Prove it.
model: Formulation 1 is stronger (the book's answer). Inclusion. If $x\ge 0$ satisfies formulation 1, then for $i\ne j$ in $C(k)$: $x_{it}+x_{jt}\le\sum_{l\in C(k)}x_{lt}\le 1$, so $x$ satisfies formulation 2: $P_1\subseteq P_2$. Strictness (as soon as a student takes at least three courses): with courses $\{1,2,3\}$ of one student and two days, set $x_{it}=\tfrac12$ for all $i,t$. Then $\sum_t x_{it}=1$ and every pair satisfies $\tfrac12+\tfrac12\le 1$, but $\sum_{i}x_{it}=\tfrac32\gt 1$: the point is in $P_2$ and not in $P_1$. Hence $P_1\subsetneq P_2$. (If every student takes at most two courses the two formulations coincide.)
rubric: States that the formulation with the sum over $C(k)$ (clique form) is the stronger one
Proves the pairwise constraints are implied by the clique constraints using $x\ge 0$
Gives a fractional point (e.g. all $x_{it}=1/2$ with three courses) feasible for the pairwise formulation
Shows this point violates a clique constraint, hence strict inclusion
explain: The clique constraint is the sum-form of all pairwise conflicts among the courses of one student; it has fewer constraints and a tighter LP relaxation.

q: Lot sizing over $T$ periods with demands $d_t\ge 0$. Formulation $P_1$ uses production $x_t\ge 0$, stock $s_t\ge 0$ and set-up $y_t\in[0,1]$ (LP relaxation) with $x_t+s_{t-1}=d_t+s_t$ for $t=1,\dots,T$, $s_0=s_T=0$, and $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$ where $M_t=\sum_{i=t}^{T}d_i$. Formulation $P_2$ uses $x_t\ge 0$, $y_t\in[0,1]$ and $w_{st}\ge 0$ ($s\le t$), the fraction of the demand of period $t$ produced in period $s$, with $x_t=\sum_{i=t}^{T}d_i\,w_{ti}$, $\sum_{s=1}^{t}w_{st}=1$ for all $t$, and $w_{st}\le y_s$. Show that every $(x,y)$ in the projection of $P_2$ belongs to the projection of $P_1$, and give a small example showing that the inclusion is strict.
model: Inclusion. Given $(x,y,w)\in P_2$, define $s_t=\sum_{r\le t}\sum_{i\gt t}d_i\,w_{ri}\ge 0$ (demand of later periods already produced), so $s_0=0$ and $s_T=0$. Then $$x_t+s_{t-1}=\sum_{r\le t}\sum_{i\ge t}d_i\,w_{ri}=d_t\sum_{r\le t}w_{rt}+s_t=d_t+s_t,$$ and $x_t=\sum_{i\ge t}d_i\,w_{ti}\le\Big(\sum_{i\ge t}d_i\Big)y_t=M_t\,y_t$. So $(x,y,s)\in P_1$. Strictness. $T=2$, $d=(1,1)$: $x=(1,1)$, $y=(\tfrac12,1)$, $s_1=0$ is in $P_1$ because $x_1=1\le M_1y_1=2\cdot\tfrac12$. In $P_2$, $w_{11}=1$ forces $y_1\ge 1$, so this $(x,y)$ is not in the projection of $P_2$. Intuition. $P_1$ uses a single big-M covering all the remaining demand, while $P_2$ links the set-up to each period's demand separately ($w_{st}\le y_s$, i.e. a big-M equal to 1 per demand).
rubric: Defines a stock $s_t$ from $w$ (demand of periods after $t$ produced up to $t$) and checks $s\ge 0$
Verifies the balance equations $x_t+s_{t-1}=d_t+s_t$ using $\sum_{s\le t}w_{st}=1$
Derives $x_t\le M_t y_t$ from $w_{ti}\le y_t$
Gives a fractional point of $P_1$ that has no preimage in $P_2$ (e.g. $T=2$, $d=(1,1)$, $y_1=1/2$)
Intuition: disaggregated big-M (one per unit of demand) versus one aggregated big-M
explain: Comparing an extended formulation with a compact one requires projecting onto the common variables $(x,y)$; exam question (January 2017) without printed solution.

q: Let $X_2=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}_+\times\{0,1\}:\ x\le 20\,y,\ x\le 5\}$ and consider the fractional point $(x,y)=(5,\tfrac14)$ of its LP relaxation. Which inequality is valid for $X_2$ and cuts off this point?
explain: Disjunction on $y$: $y=0$ forces $x=0$ and $y=1$ allows $x\le 5$, so $x\le 5y$ is valid (the big-M 20 is tightened to 5). At the point: $5\gt 5\cdot\tfrac14$, so it is cut off. $x\le 20y$ holds with equality at the point; $x\le 4y$ is not valid ($(5,1)\in X_2$); $x+15y\le 20$ is valid but satisfied by the point ($8.75\le 20$). The same reasoning gives $x\le 7y$ for $\{x\le 20y,\ x\le 7\}$ (book, ex. 5.1.1).

q: Undirected TSP on $G=(V,E)$ with $x_e\in[0,1]$ and degree constraints $\sum_{e\in\delta(i)}x_e=2$ for all $i\in V$. Show that for every $S\subsetneq V$ with $2\le|S|\le|V|-1$ the subtour-elimination constraint $\sum_{e\in E(S)}x_e\le|S|-1$ holds if and only if the cut-set constraint $\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge 2$ holds. What does this imply for the two formulations $P_{sub}$ and $P_{cut}$?
model: Sum the degree constraints over $i\in S$: an edge with both ends in $S$ is counted twice and an edge of the cut once, so $$2|S|=2\,x(E(S))+x(\delta(S)).$$ Therefore $x(E(S))\le|S|-1\iff 2|S|-x(\delta(S))\le 2|S|-2\iff x(\delta(S))\ge 2$. Given the degree equations, the two constraints for the same $S$ are equivalent, so $P_{sub}=P_{cut}$: the LP relaxations coincide and neither formulation is stronger. Both families contain exponentially many constraints and are handled by separation (lazy constraints).
rubric: Sums the degree constraints over the vertices of $S$
Obtains $2|S|=2x(E(S))+x(\delta(S))$ (inside edges counted twice, cut edges once)
Deduces the equivalence of the two inequalities for each $S$
Concludes $P_{sub}=P_{cut}$ (same LP relaxation)
explain: The book prints the partition $\delta(S)=E(V)\setminus E(S)\setminus E(V\setminus S)$ and leaves the conclusion to the reader; the counting identity above is the key step.

q: What distinguishes lazy constraints from user cuts in a MIP solver?
options: User cuts are needed for correctness, whereas lazy constraints only speed up the solver
Lazy constraints may only remove fractional solutions, whereas user cuts may remove integer-feasible solutions

Lazy constraints belong to the formulation (they are needed for correctness) and may cut off integer points feasible for the current model; user cuts only strengthen the relaxation and may remove only fractional points
There is no difference: both are optional strengthening inequalities
explain: Lazy constraints are constraints of the model that are left out because there are too many (e.g. subtour-elimination or cut-set constraints of the TSP) and are added back when violated; without them the model is wrong, so they must be allowed to reject integer solutions. User cuts are valid inequalities added in callbacks at branch-and-bound nodes: they never remove feasible integer solutions, only fractional ones.
